entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Workers' Party (Partido dos Trabalhadores, PT) of Brazil, founded in 1980 by trade union leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is Latin America's most electorally successful left-wing party and the political vehicle that lifted 20 million Brazilians out of poverty under Lula's presidency (2003-2010) while achieving unprecedented GDP growth. The PT's Bolsa Família conditional cash transfer program — which reached 14 million families — became the global template for poverty reduction programs adopted in over 50 countries.

Lula da Silva, a steelworker who lost his left thumb in a factory accident and never attended university, founded the PT from within São Paulo's industrial labor unions. The party rejected alliance with the traditional Brazilian left and built a new working-class base from the ABC São Paulo metalworkers' strikes of 1979-1980. Lula ran for president four times (1989, 1994, 1998, losing each time) before winning in 2002 — the longest political persistence of any democratic leader before eventual victory.

Under Lula's first presidency (2003-2010), Brazil grew at 7.5% GDP growth, inflation fell, and the 20 million poverty reduction was celebrated globally. The PT's 2012 corruption scandal (Mensalão) and the 2016 Petrobras/Lava Jato investigation led to Dilma Rousseff's impeachment and Lula's 2018 imprisonment — before his conviction was annulled and he returned to win a third term in 2022, defeating Jair Bolsonaro. Lula's personal trajectory — from imprisoned factory worker to three-term president — is one of democracy's most remarkable stories.
